claim: Did you know… standing like Wonder Woman for two minutes raises your testosterone?

studies.finding: Two minutes in expansive poses was reported to raise testosterone, lower cortisol, and increase risk-taking relative to contracted poses.
studies.verdict: Cited as the origin of the claim; later work did not hold it up.

studies.finding: A larger replication found higher self-reported power after expansive poses, but no hormone or behavioral differences.
studies.verdict: Feelings only; hormone and behavior effects absent.

claim: Did you know… resisting a plate of cookies leaves you with less willpower afterward?

studies.cite: Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven & Tice (1998), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Participants who resisted tempting chocolates gave up sooner on an unsolvable puzzle, which was read as depleted self-control.
studies.verdict: Foundational ego depletion study; the effect has not survived large replications.

studies.cite: Hagger et al. (2016), Perspectives on Psychological Science
studies.finding: Twenty-three labs (N = 2,141) ran a standardized depletion protocol and pooled a small effect with a confidence interval including zero.
studies.verdict: Registered Replication Report: d = 0.04, interval includes zero.

studies.finding: A preregistered 36-lab study (N = 3,531) tested depletion with two procedures and found no significant effect.
studies.verdict: Confirmatory test d = 0.06, nonsignificant; authors found no evidence of depletion.

claim: Did you know… reading words about old age makes you walk more slowly?

studies.cite: Bargh, Chen & Burrows (1996), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Students unscrambling elderly-related words walked more slowly down a hallway afterward than students given neutral words.
studies.verdict: Landmark priming result; direct replication did not reproduce it.

studies.finding: With automated infrared timing, no slowing appeared; it showed up only when experimenters were led to expect it.
studies.verdict: Failed with objective timing; effect tracked experimenter expectation.

claim: Did you know… holding a pen in your teeth makes cartoons funnier?

studies.cite: Strack, Martin & Stepper (1988), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: People holding a pen with their teeth, forcing a smile, rated cartoons as funnier than those holding it with their lips.
studies.verdict: Original finding; replications have since split.

studies.cite: Wagenmakers et al. (2016), Perspectives on Psychological Science
studies.finding: Seventeen labs repeated the pen-in-mouth cartoon study and found no systematic effect of facial feedback.
studies.verdict: Registered Replication Report: original effect not reproduced.

studies.cite: Coles et al. (2022), Nature Human Behaviour
studies.finding: Across 19 countries (N = 3,878), mimicry and voluntary facial actions shifted happiness; the pen-in-mouth task was less conclusive.
studies.verdict: Some facial feedback effects appear; the pen task remains inconclusive.

claim: Did you know… hurricanes with feminine names kill more people than masculine-named ones?

studies.finding: Archival data on US hurricanes suggested feminine-named storms caused more deaths, which the authors tied to weaker perceived threat.
studies.verdict: Original claim; reanalyses question the modeling.

studies.finding: After removing damages from the model and controlling for population at risk, the name effect was not robust and sometimes reversed.
studies.verdict: Reanalysis: effect not robust to specification.

studies.finding: A reanalysis argued the original regression was fragile and the data contain no evidence that feminine names cause more deaths.
studies.verdict: Letter: data do not support a causal name effect.

claim: Did you know… people named Dennis are disproportionately likely to become dentists?

studies.cite: Pelham, Mirenberg & Jones (2002), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Archival records showed people choose careers, cities and spouses resembling their own names more often than chance would predict.
studies.verdict: Original implicit egotism evidence.

studies.cite: Simonsohn (2011), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
studies.finding: Reanalysis argued the name-matching patterns are most likely produced by cohort, geographic and ethnic confounds, plus reverse causality.
studies.verdict: Critique says confounds explain it; authors dispute this.

claim: Did you know… a four-year-old's wait for a marshmallow predicts later achievement?

studies.finding: Preschoolers who delayed gratification longer were later rated more competent and scored higher on the SAT.
studies.verdict: Real association, but small sample and no family controls.

studies.finding: In a larger, more diverse sample the link was about half as large and shrank by two-thirds with family controls.
studies.verdict: Association largely reflects family background and early ability.

claim: Did you know… basketball's hot hand is a statistical illusion that fools fans?

studies.finding: Analysis of 76ers shooting records found no evidence that a made shot makes the next one more likely.
studies.verdict: Famous null result, later shown to rest on a biased test.

studies.finding: Selecting shots that follow streaks biases the measured hit rate downward; correcting this reverses the 1985 conclusion.
studies.verdict: Selection bias found; corrected data show streak shooting.

claim: Did you know… students role-playing prison guards spontaneously turned cruel?

studies.cite: Haney, Banks & Zimbardo (1973), International Journal of Criminology and Penology
studies.finding: Volunteers assigned guard and prisoner roles in a mock prison reportedly showed rapid, severe behavioral change within days.
studies.verdict: Original report; the conclusion is now heavily disputed.

studies.finding: Archival review argued the guards were coached and understood what was expected, undermining the claim of spontaneous cruelty.
studies.verdict: Archives suggest guards were coached; Zimbardo and colleagues dispute the critique.

claim: Did you know… listening to Mozart makes you smarter?

studies.finding: College students scored higher on a spatial reasoning task after listening to a Mozart sonata than after silence or relaxation tapes.
studies.verdict: A brief task-specific effect, later inflated into general intelligence.

studies.finding: A meta-analysis of 39 studies found small effects, with larger ones in affiliated labs and strong evidence of publication bias.
studies.verdict: Meta-analysis: little evidence for any special Mozart effect.

claim: Did you know… a random number shifts your guess of Chicago's population?

studies.cite: Jacowitz & Kahneman (1995), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
studies.finding: Estimates of quantities were pulled toward arbitrary high or low numbers participants had just compared them with.
studies.verdict: Original anchoring result; it has been strongly replicated.

studies.finding: Across 36 samples, all four anchoring tests were significant in the expected direction, with effects larger than the original.
studies.verdict: Many Labs: replicated in every sample, with larger effects.

claim: Did you know… most ordinary people will give painful shocks when an experimenter insists?

studies.cite: Milgram (1963), Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
studies.finding: In the original obedience study, every participant reached 300 volts and 65% continued to the maximum 450 volts.
studies.verdict: Original study; its basic finding has been reproduced in modified form.

studies.finding: A partial replication halting at 150 volts found obedience rates virtually identical to Milgram's at that point.
studies.verdict: Replicated under modern ethics limits, with a truncated protocol.

studies.cite: Doliński et al. (2017), Social Psychological and Personality Science
studies.finding: In Poland, 90% of 80 participants were willing to press the highest of ten lower-voltage buttons.
studies.verdict: Obedience again comparable to Milgram's; sample small, shocks reduced.
